title: Native PDF viewing
subtitle: Decision walkthrough · 10 Nov 2026 · narrated by Duo's house voice
posterLine: What the research found about PDFs in Duo, then four decisions. Tap play and listen; it stops when it needs you.
footer: Built with the decision-walkthrough skill from docs/research/pdf-viewing-walkthrough/spec.json. Answers are saved in this page and sent to director-duo-v2.

said.PDF.js: P D F dot J S

lines.text: You asked for native PDF viewing, so here's what I found, and four decisions.
Today a PDF opens in Quick Look, under a read-only strip.
It draws the page well. But it can't tell Duo which page you're on, or what you've selected. So nothing else can build on it.
You asked three things. Where it opens, how Claude reads all of it, and comments that travel with the file.
I made a hundred and twenty page test file, with charts, two columns, a table and a scanned page.
Claude Code's Read took the whole thing in one call, every page as text and a picture. That's something like two to three hundred thousand tokens.
Pulling just the text took seven hundredths of a second, and about a sixth of the tokens.
But text loses the numbers in the charts, and the scanned page entirely.
Text plus pictures of only the thirteen pages that need them lost nothing, at about fifty four thousand.
The PDF standard already has threaded comments. A highlight or a sticky note, with the author's name.
A reply points back at it, and resolving is a hidden status reply marked Completed.
Apple's PDFKit writes notes and highlights fine, but it can't write a reply, and every save rewrites the whole file.
So I wrote a small appender. It added a reply and a status in seven hundred bytes, after the original, which stays untouched.
Acrobat reads that model, and PDF.js shows the reply.

chapters.title: What draws the PDF
chapters.ask: What should draw a PDF in the editor area?
chapters.why: Quick Look can't see the page or the selection, so it can't host Send Selection, duo2 page verbs or comments.

lines.text: First decision. What draws the PDF.
I recommend Apple's PDFKit. It's Preview's renderer, it's already in Duo, and it opened the test file in six hundredths of a second.

options.label: PDFKit, native
options.desc: Preview's renderer, already linked; zoom, find and selection built in. Needs a native PageHost for Send Selection. About 3–4 days after the bar is designed.

lines.text: Option one, PDFKit. Zoom, find and selection come free. The work is teaching Duo's send and picker plumbing about a native view. Three or four days, after a design round.

options.label: PDF.js in a web view
options.desc: Like the Word and PowerPoint viewers. Reuses the picker; adds 13 MB and a second PDF engine; shows no review status.

lines.text: Option two, PDF.js in a web view, like the Word and PowerPoint viewers. The picker comes along, but it's thirteen megabytes and a second engine, and it hides review status.

options.label: Keep Quick Look, add a bar
options.desc: Cheapest. Still blind to the page and the selection, so no comments.

lines.text: Option three keeps Quick Look. Cheapest, but still blind, so no comments.

chapters.title: PDFs in split view
chapters.ask: Can a PDF be one side of a split view?
chapters.why: Split view takes only text files today; PDFs, Word documents and decks are all refused, so PowerPoint isn't in split view yet either.

lines.text: Next, split view. You mentioned PowerPoint opens there, but today split view only takes text, so decks and Word files are refused too.
I recommend letting a PDF sit beside a text document, so you can read the paper and write the notes.

options.label: A PDF beside a text document
options.desc: View-only side; the text side keeps the editor. Decide decks and Word with it. About a day after the viewer.

lines.text: Option one. The PDF is the view-only side, about a day of work after the viewer, and decks and Word documents could follow the same rule.

options.label: Split view stays text-only
options.desc: A PDF opens as its own tab; a session can sit in the other pane.

lines.text: Option two keeps split view for text, and the PDF opens as its own tab.

chapters.title: What Claude reads
chapters.ask: What does a Claude session get when it reads a PDF?
chapters.why: Read on the whole PDF costs about 180k–360k tokens for 120 pages; text alone loses charts and scans.

look.label: §4 of the research: the agent reads the whole PDF

lines.text: Third, what a Claude session gets.
I recommend duo2 doc read returns the text with page markers, then names the pages to look at as pictures, like charts and scans.

options.label: Text with page markers, plus the pages to view
options.desc: duo2 doc read: about 54k tokens on the fixture, nothing lost. The path is in the payload too. About a day.

lines.text: Option one. Claude reads only the pages it's pointed at. About fifty four thousand tokens, nothing lost, and a day of work.

options.label: Just the path
options.desc: Read takes every page as an image: complete, but several times the tokens, and it may not fit a 200k context.

lines.text: Option two hands over just the path. Complete, but several times the tokens.

options.label: Convert to Markdown
options.desc: docling or MarkItDown: better structure, but heavy (PyTorch) or weak (no layout).

lines.text: Option three converts it to Markdown with an outside tool. Better structure, but heavy.

chapters.title: Where comments live
chapters.ask: Where do a PDF's comments live, and how are they written?
chapters.why: Portable means other apps see them: in the PDF, in the standard's own form. PDFKit can't write replies and rewrites the file.

lines.text: Last, where comments live.
I recommend keeping them inside the PDF, in the form the standard defines, added after the original bytes, so a signature still holds.

options.label: In the PDF, appended by Duo
options.desc: Standard annotations: replies by /IRT, Resolve as a /State reply. Read with CGPDF, written by Duo's incremental writer; PDFKit only draws. @claude as in DL-236. About 6–9 days with the margin UI.

lines.text: Option one. Add, reply and resolve map straight onto the standard, and at-Claude works as it does in Markdown. Six to nine days, including the margin.

options.label: An XFDF sidecar beside the PDF
options.desc: The PDF is never touched; Acrobat can import it. Lost when the PDF is sent alone. Better as an export.

lines.text: Option two keeps them in a file beside the PDF. Safe, but they're lost when the PDF is sent alone.

options.label: PDFKit's own save
options.desc: Least code, but it rewrites the whole file, breaks signatures, and can't write replies.

lines.text: Option three uses PDFKit's own save. It's the smallest amount of code, but no replies, and it rewrites the whole file.
That's all four decisions.
Each answer went to the director as you saved it, and Copy decisions puts them all on the clipboard.
Whatever you pick, the viewer's bar and the comment margin need a design round before anything is built.
